unit: Week 1 — Studio 1: Begin with your curiosity
title: Your arm and your research assistant, not your brain: the course promise and a live citation-catch
driving_question: What does research even mean when an AI can generate the code and the prose for you?
secondary_questions: What will you build this semester? Where is the line between AI assistance and intellectual substitution? What does 'AI may propose, the researcher must verify' demand of you on day one?
claim_permitted: "An AI tool generated this, the source exists, and I read, confirmed, and criticized the underlying argument or technique before using it" — the course's opening standard.
claim_not_permitted: "The AI said so" offered as evidence — a generated citation you have not retrieved and checked is not yet a source.
rdss_reading: RDSS ch. 1 (Preface) + ch. 2 'What is a research design?' — skim before Wednesday (book.declaredesign.org)
other_material: nb01 (Colab); course website; syllabus; Brightspace orientation; genai.rcac.purdue.edu login
provenance: brief §Week1 + RDSS ch.2 | research in the age of AI | course promise + live AI citation-catch + Colab/GenAI Studio readiness | newly-constructed-from-source-concept
concepts: evidence-driven research; AI as arm and research assistant, not brain; assistance vs intellectual substitution; hallucination; the AI Research Ledger (preview); Ask -> Verify -> Document (the everyday form of SDIIVDD); the weekly rhythm (lectures + Friday studio)
python_r_dependency: Colab basics only (run a cell, save a copy to Drive)
dataset_simulation: none (one live AI-generated citation to verify)
minute_dynamic: 0–9 instructor-led puzzle: what is left for a researcher to do once an AI can write the code and the prose? — the class maps the answer on the board; 9–31 guided AI research-partner investigation in nb01: ask AI for three sources on a shared question and open each one, watching one citation fail to resolve; 31–43 human verification + instructor formalization: run the failed citation through the verification checklist, name hallucination and the arm-not-brain principle, and set up the AI Research Ledger; 43–50 decision & defense: log the caught citation as the first Ledger entry + Claim Ticket.
hands_on_activity: Open nb01 in Colab, save a copy to Drive, ask AI for sources on a shared question, and catch the one citation that will not resolve using the verification checklist.
practice: 📝 nb01 practice: for three AI-generated claims, mark which you could defend right now and which need a source you would have to retrieve first.
discussion_prompt: When has a confident answer, from a person or a tool, turned out to be wrong for you — and what would have caught it earlier?
project_connection: The semester project starts today: everyone leaves set up in Colab, logged into the course tools, and holding the M0 baseline assignment.
milestone_developed: M0 — Research and AI baseline, Book Milestone 1 v1 (kickoff)
milestone_work_time: 5 min (M0 brief walkthrough + first baseline-belief jotting)
milestone_presentation_review: none (kickoff)
student_prep: Bring a laptop; be able to log into Google (Colab), Brightspace, and genai.rcac.purdue.edu.
student_artifact: Executed nb01 readiness cells + first AI Research Ledger entry (the caught citation)
exit_ticket: Claim Ticket #1: one thing you assume AI is good at in research, and how you would check whether it actually is.
homework_next_milestone: Start M0 (baseline beliefs about AI, three curiosities, tool-readiness screenshots, first Ledger entries) — due at this Friday's studio, where you pitch one curiosity in 30 seconds. Skim RDSS ch. 1–2 before Wednesday.
instructor_prep: Verify nb01 loads in Colab from the public repo; rehearse the live AI citation-catch and keep an offline screenshot backup; confirm GenAI Studio logins work; roster the 5 students.
risks_contingency: AI returns only valid citations in the live demo → fall back to the saved transcript of a prior hallucination and have the class verify it; account/Colab issues → pair on one laptop and finish readiness at home.

unit: Week 1 — Studio 1: Begin with your curiosity
title: Automation bias, false confidence, and the first full Ask -> Verify -> Document cycle
driving_question: Why do smart people trust a wrong machine, and what discipline keeps you from joining them?
secondary_questions: What is automation bias? How does fluent AI prose manufacture false confidence and the illusion of understanding? Which research decisions must stay human? What are the seven moves of Specify -> Delegate -> Interrogate -> Inspect -> Verify -> Document -> Defend?
claim_permitted: "I delegated this step, interrogated the output, and verified it against a source I can point to" — a claim that survives the full cycle.
claim_not_permitted: "It sounded right and detailed, so I used it" — fluency is not evidence, and detail is not verification.
rdss_reading: RDSS ch. 2 'What is a research design?' (finish; book.declaredesign.org)
other_material: nb01 §Lecture 2 (Colab); the AI Research Ledger template
provenance: brief §Week1 + RDSS ch.2 | research in the age of AI | automation-bias framing + first full SDIIVDD cycle on a toy claim | newly-constructed-from-source-concept
concepts: automation bias; false confidence; the illusion of understanding; assistance vs substitution; research ownership + human decision authority; the never-delegate list; SDIIVDD (Specify -> Delegate -> Interrogate -> Inspect -> Verify -> Document -> Defend) and its shorthand Ask -> Verify -> Document; the AI Research Ledger fields
python_r_dependency: Colab (run provided cells; no new libraries)
dataset_simulation: none (one toy factual claim carried through the full cycle)
minute_dynamic: 0–7 instructor-led retrieval & challenge: name yesterday's arm-not-brain principle and one decision an AI must never make for you; 7–30 intensive applied AI laboratory: run the SCORED S2 colleague audit on the shared declared-question card (commit → locate → verify → diagnose → repair → calibrate), then take one toy claim through all seven SDIIVDD moves in nb01 — specify the task, delegate it to AI, interrogate and inspect the output, then verify it against a real source and document the Ledger row; 30–38 peer defense + adversarial questioning: partners try to break each other's verification ("how do you KNOW the source says that?"); 38–42 synthesis + instructor accuracy lock (modeled): state the room's conclusion and its uncertainty, and correct anything wrong before it enters a ledger, naming the move so leads can replicate it; 42–50 transfer to the final project + Ledger + Claim Ticket.
hands_on_activity: Run one toy claim through all seven SDIIVDD moves in nb01 and fill a complete AI Research Ledger row, ending with a source you personally opened.
practice: 📝 nb01 practice: match five research tasks to 'safe to delegate', 'delegate then verify', or 'never delegate', and justify each in a phrase.
discussion_prompt: Describe a time a detailed, confident explanation made you stop checking. What would automation bias look like in your own project?
project_connection: The Ledger row you complete today is the template for every AI use you will document in the project dossier.
milestone_developed: M0 — Research and AI baseline, Book Milestone 1 v1 (dev)
milestone_work_time: 5 min (draft one real Ledger entry from your own AI use this week)
milestone_presentation_review: none (baseline is a studio submission)
student_prep: M0 in progress (baseline beliefs + curiosities started); RDSS ch. 2 skimmed; laptop ready.
student_artifact: One complete AI Research Ledger row (task, tool, prompt, output, decision, verification, remaining concern)
exit_ticket: Claim Ticket #2: one AI output you trusted this week, and the exact check that would confirm or break it.
homework_next_milestone: Finish M0 (baseline AI beliefs, three curiosities, tool-readiness screenshots, first Ledger entries) for this Friday's studio, where you pitch one curiosity in 30 seconds.
instructor_prep: Prepare the toy-claim cycle end-to-end in nb01; print the SDIIVDD and never-delegate cards; review any early M0 drafts.
risks_contingency: The cycle runs long → verify and document the toy claim together as a class and move peer defense to a written exchange; keep the never-delegate list visible as the anchor.

unit: Week 2 — Studio 2: Govern the work and declare your question
title: From curiosity to a research problem: the funnel, and what makes a problem worth doing
driving_question: How does a curiosity become a research problem someone would fund a semester of your life to study?
secondary_questions: What separates a topic from a research problem from a question? What do importance, feasibility, and contribution each demand? What are units of analysis, target populations, and outcomes?

claim_permitted: "My problem names its units, its outcome, and the population it speaks to, and I can say why it matters and why it is doable this semester."
claim_not_permitted: "My topic is important, so any question about it is a research problem" — a topic is a subject, a problem is a specific gap someone could act on.

unit: Week 2 — Studio 2: Govern the work and declare your question
title: The inquiry compass: descriptive, predictive, or causal — kind x reach
driving_question: What KIND of answer does your question ask for, and how far is it trying to reach?
secondary_questions: How do descriptive, predictive, and causal questions differ? Why is prediction a descriptive question about unseen cases, not a causal one? What goes wrong when a single question tries to do two jobs at once?
inquiry: all four compass positions (the compass skill)
srl_slot: SRL slot 02 (randomly assigned at semester start)
srl_focus: Puzzle: one question secretly asks two things at once (what is happening AND what would fix it) — where does it split, and which half is which kind?
claim_permitted: "My question is a ___ inquiry reaching ___ (data at hand / a population / unseen cases), because the answer it wants is ___."
claim_not_permitted: A question that fuses description and causation in one breath ("how common is burnout and does remote work cause it?") pretending to be a single answerable question.
rdss_reading: RDSS ch. 7 'Defining the inquiry' (descriptive vs causal inquiries; book.declaredesign.org)
cb_reading: optional: callingbullshit.org case on prediction vs understanding
other_material: nb02 §Lecture 2 (Colab)
provenance: RDSS ch.7 + fresh compass build | defining the inquiry | kind x reach compass with the prediction column authored fresh (descriptive about unseen cases) | extended
concepts: the inquiry compass: kind (descriptive vs causal) x reach (data at hand / population / unseen); the four positions — description, generalization, prediction, causal reasoning; prediction as descriptive questions about unseen cases; questions that improperly combine objectives; the giveaway words that place a question
python_r_dependency: none (classification in markdown cells)
dataset_simulation: none (question cards spanning the compass)
minute_dynamic: 0–7 SRL-led retrieval & challenge: name the compass axes from memory, then the SRL reveals one question that secretly asks two things; 7–30 intensive applied AI laboratory: in nb02, classify a deck of question cards by kind and reach, then ask AI to classify the same cards and adjudicate every disagreement against the definitions; 30–38 peer defense + adversarial questioning: classify YOUR own question and defend its position while a partner tries to move it; 38–42 SRL synthesis + instructor accuracy lock: the lead states the room's conclusion and its uncertainty, and the instructor corrects any claim that survived challenge but is wrong before it can enter a ledger; 42–50 transfer to the final project + Ledger + Claim Ticket.
hands_on_activity: Classify a deck of question cards by kind and reach, pit your classification against AI's, and resolve every disagreement with the definitions — then place your own question.
practice: 📝 nb02 practice: for eight questions, name the kind + reach AND rewrite the one that improperly combines two objectives into two clean questions.
discussion_prompt: Why is 'predicting who will drop out' a descriptive question about unseen cases and not a causal one, and what would make it causal?
project_connection: Each student leaves with a first compass position for their own question, recorded in the M1 landscape.

unit: Week 3 — Studio 3: Ground it in verified evidence
title: Research builds on research: verified evidence, citation chains, and real gaps
driving_question: How do you find what is actually known, prove each source is real, and tell a genuine gap from a search you simply gave up on?
secondary_questions: How is a field a cumulative conversation (replication, extension, synthesis, comparison, boundary conditions)? What are forward and backward citation searches? Why must every citation be retrieved and its claim checked before you use it?
srl_slot: SRL slot 03 (randomly assigned at semester start)
srl_focus: Puzzle: an AI hands you a perfect-sounding study you cannot find anywhere — is the gap real, or did the search just fail?
claim_permitted: "Source S exists, I retrieved it, and it claims X on the basis of evidence E" — and "across the sources I checked, no one has addressed C."
claim_not_permitted: "Nothing is known about my topic" from a search that stopped early, or citing any source you have not personally opened — however fluent the AI summary.
rdss_reading: RDSS ch. 4 'Getting started' (situating a design in a literature; book.declaredesign.org) + course library-search guidance
other_material: nb03 (Colab); Purdue Libraries database portal; Google Scholar
provenance: RDSS ch.4 + fresh AI-era source-verification method | getting started | retrieval-verification loop + citation-chain search + evidence map, tuned for an AI-assisted honors audience | newly-constructed-from-source-concept
concepts: research as cumulative conversation; replication, extension, synthesis, comparison, boundary conditions; backward and forward citation searches; the retrieval-verification loop (retrieve it, confirm it exists, log how you checked); claim–evidence–source alignment; citation hallucination; mischaracterized sources; genuine gap vs unsuccessful search; the evidence map

minute_dynamic: 0–7 SRL-led retrieval & challenge: the SRL presents an AI-surfaced study nobody can locate and the class decides what that means; 7–30 intensive applied AI laboratory: first the SCORED S3 colleague audit on your colleague's evidence registry (one source does not support its claim — find it, verify it, repair it), then, for YOUR question, run one AI search and one library-database search, retrieve every source, verify each is real, log its central claim, and follow one backward and one forward citation link; 30–38 peer defense + adversarial questioning: swap evidence maps and challenge whether each placed gap is genuine or just an unfinished search; 38–42 SRL synthesis + instructor accuracy lock: the lead states the room's conclusion and its uncertainty, and the instructor corrects any claim that survived challenge but is wrong before it can enter a ledger; 42–50 transfer to the final project + Ledger + Claim Ticket.

discussion_prompt: An AI summary cites a perfect study you cannot find. What are the three possible explanations, and what do you do next?
project_connection: The verified evidence and the provisional gap started today are the backbone of M2, due at this Friday's studio.

unit: Week 4 — Studio 4: Declare and diagnose provisionally
title: The anatomy of a research design: MIDA — Model, Inquiry, Data strategy, Answer strategy
driving_question: What are the four parts every research design must have, and what must the world be like for your question to have an answer?
secondary_questions: What is a model, and how does a DAG say 'I believe X could affect Y'? What is an inquiry (estimand), and why must it be named before data arrive? What does it mean for the four MIDA parts to align?
srl_slot: SRL slot 04 (randomly assigned at semester start)

secondary_questions: Do the remaining defenses survive cross-examination? Is the dossier complete and every ledger closed as a record, not a summary? Can you say your stopping rule aloud — and what should the next study ask?
claim_permitted: "My release audit passed, my last cold run is not stale, my stopping rule is stated as a decision, and I can defend every claim from a verified ledger."
claim_not_permitted: "The AI wrote my chapter" (you directed, verified, and own it — or you did not, and the defense shows which).

concepts: the Evidence Defense under cross-examination; the release ceremony; the closed dossier and closed ledgers (complete records, not summaries); the AI-management portfolio (what was automated, escalated, and overridden); the stopping rule said aloud; the next-study agenda (a research cycle ends by declaring the next one); number-to-cell traceability; verification as a habit that outlasts the course

dataset_simulation: each student's own chapter, dossier, ledgers, and AI-management portfolio
minute_dynamic: 0–10 weekly topic quiz: five multiple-choice questions on the week's topic, answered solo on paper and handed in; 10–15 research stand-up: the AI decision you are proudest of overruling, one line each; 15–45 milestone kickoff + defense rounds: the instructor runs the release checklist one last time (stale-run status, the five audit parts, the dossier manifest), then the REMAINING EVIDENCE DEFENSES run as the work block in the drawn order (compressed staging so all five defenders fit across the two meetings), every non-defender asking at least one ledger-grounded question, and each defender closing with the stopping rule said aloud and the next-study agenda in one sentence; 45–50 revise, ledger, submit + Claim Ticket: submit M15 and confirm it on screen, take the reflection survey, and write the final Claim Ticket.
hands_on_activity: Deliver or cross-examine the final defenses, run a last stale-run and traceability spot-check on your own chapter, and release: submit M15.
practice: 📝 (retrospective) the exit self-assessment: classify, match, bound, verify, release — rate yourself at the start of the semester versus now.
discussion_prompt: What claim did you believe at the start of the semester that you would now demand evidence for, and what evidence would satisfy you?
project_connection: M15 — the release audit, final chapter, closed dossier, and AI-management portfolio — is submitted; the semester's complete, defended, reproducible artifact leaves your hands pointing at its successor.
milestone_developed: M15 — Release audit, final chapter, and AI-management portfolio, Book Milestone 12 v1 (worked + due TONIGHT — TERMINAL, no revision window)
milestone_work_time: 30 min studio block (final defenses + release ceremony)
milestone_presentation_review: the remaining Evidence Defenses ARE the presentation/review
student_prep: Chapter, dossier, and AI-management portfolio complete; package cold run fresh (not stale); ready to defend or cross-examine.
student_artifact: Delivered defense or logged cross-examination + submitted M15 + exit self-assessment + reflection survey
exit_ticket: Claim Ticket #43 (the last): one claim I will carry carefully for the rest of my life, and the evidence I hold it on.
homework_next_milestone: None. It is done. The next-study agenda you wrote is where the cycle reopens, whenever you choose. (Grades follow the posted rubric timeline.)
instructor_prep: Rubrics per remaining defender; the overflow slot in reserve; the strongest-defenses synthesis list; survey link live; submission mechanics confirmed; celebration logistics.
risks_contingency: A chapter misses the ceremony → the tonight deadline governs and the published late policy applies; a defense needs the full length → the office-hours overflow slot absorbs it before the deadline; a last-minute stale run → release with the rerun queued and DECLARED, never silently stale.
